articles.title: How One Lawyer Built A 7-Figure Practice Without A ‘Networking’ Mindset
articles.content:
在与Kalmanson Cohen PLLC劳动与雇佣诉讼律师Randi Cohen的交谈中，我探讨了一位拥有近20年经验的律师如何在几乎不自称擅长人脉建设的情况下，建立起一家七位数的律所。Randi分享了她如何直面冒牌者综合征，通过真诚的好奇心建立关系，并逐渐意识到曾经令她畏惧的人可以成为最忠诚的支持者。

**对抗"冒牌者综合征"**
Randi曾面对试图吓唬她团队的强势对手。表面上，她的团队坚定不移，但内心却备受煎熬。而那个曾试图威胁她的对手，现在竟成了她的推荐来源。

**分享真实的自己**
Randi对业务发展的首要建议是什么？深入了解客户，甚至包括对手。她解释了原因。

**不以"人脉建设"之名**
Randi分享了她对人脉建设的独特理解，或者说，她根本不这样思考。核心理念简单明了：倾听他人真实需求，以慷慨之心为先。当业务发展建立在这一基础上时，一切将变得简单。

Steve Fretzin是五届畅销书作者、BE THAT LAWYER和Future Rainmakers播客主持人，也是专门为律师服务的业务发展教练。超过18年，他通过"零销售式推销™"方法帮助律师无需推销、演讲或追逐，建立强大的客户群。他的客户不断成为顶尖业务开拓者，并将业务增长归功于他的教练技巧和系统。可直接通过steve@fretzin.com或网站bethatlawyer.com与他联系，或在LinkedIn添加：https://www.linkedin.com/in/stevefretzin。他的全新BE THAT LAWYER社区正在改变律师发展法学院未教授的技能。详情请访问bethatlawyer.com/community。

《一位律师如何在不以"人脉建设"思维的情况下建立七位数律所》原文刊登于Above the Law。
articles.summary:
In a recent conversation with Randi Cohen, labor and employment litigator at Kalmanson Cohen PLLC, I explored how a lawyer with nearly two decades of experience built a seven-figure practice without ever really thinking of herself as someone who networks.

Randy shared a story of imposter syndrome faced head-on, relationships built through genuine curiosity, and the slow, gratifying realization that the people you once feared can become your most loyal advocates.

Battling the ‘Imposter Complex’

Randi once faced an adversary who tried to intimidate her team. On the outside, her team held firm, but on the inside, they were sweating through it.

The adversary who tried to intimidate them? She’s now a referral source.

‘Sharing Yourself’

Randi’s No. 1 tip for business development?

Getting to know her clients — and even her adversaries. Here’s why.

Networking Without ‘Networking’

Randy shared her philosophy on networking itself, or more precisely, her refusal to think of it that way at all.

The through line is simple: listen to what people actually need, and lead with generosity. Business development becomes far less complicated when it’s grounded in this approach.

Steve Fretzin is a five-time bestselling author, host of the BE THAT LAWYER and Future Rainmakers podcasts, and a business development coach who works exclusively with attorneys. For more than 18 years, he has helped lawyers build strong books of business without selling, pitching, or chasing, using his proven Sales-Free Selling™ approach. His clients consistently become top rainmakers and credit his coaching and systems for driving meaningful, measurable growth. Steve can be reached directly at steve@fretzin.com, or through his website at bethatlawyer.com. Connect with him on LinkedIn at https://www.linkedin.com/in/stevefretzin. His ALL NEW BE THAT LAWYER Community is changing how lawyers develop the skills never taught in law school. Learn more at bethatlawyer.com/community.

The post How One Lawyer Built A 7-Figure Practice Without A ‘Networking’ Mindset appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: What’s In Your Lane?
articles.content:
在公司内部法律顾问的职业生涯中，经常会听到这样的建议：要成为企业合作伙伴，参与决策，理解业务并提供超越法律风险评估的价值。确实，优秀的内部法律顾问都能做到这些。然而，这种建议背后隐藏着一个鲜少被提及的困境——当你越来越深入业务时，越难以划清界限，尤其是你作为律师的职业伦理边界。

何时保持沉默？何时发声？这些选择往往困扰着内部法律顾问。在会议中，当某个业务决策涉及合规问题，或既不明显违法又不完全正确时，律师需要权衡会议氛围、关系网络，以及是否值得此时提出异议。这种微妙的权衡是职业中最具挑战性的部分之一，而解决方案并非一成不变。

《律师职业行为规则》第2.1条为律师提供了基本准则：要求律师在执业中保持独立的专业判断，并提供坦诚的建议。注释明确指出，律师不应因建议不讨当事人喜欢而退缩。因此，"何时发声"不仅是战略问题，更是伦理问题。当你的独立判断表明当事人需要听取建议时，你有义务表达。

并非所有问题都值得争论。内部法律顾问的有效性在于理解比例原则——选择最重要的战场进行较量，并为其他问题寻找务实的解决方案。然而，比例原则也有其限度。某些问题不可妥协。区分"可以接受"与"无法为之背书"的能力，是随着经验逐渐培养的，有时甚至需要付出代价。

内部法律顾问与外部律师在面对当事人坚持的不当行为时，选择截然不同。外部律师可以选择退出；而内部律师的选择则复杂得多。你无法辞退你唯一的当事人。即使用人单位辞退你，你的职业伦理义务仍然存在。

《律师职业行为规则》第1.13条体现了这一现实。组织是你的当事人，而非日常运营中的个人。当内部律师得知组织成员的行为违反法律义务且可能给组织造成重大损害时，必须采取行动。义务要求向上级报告，必要时甚至要向最高管理层通报。如果最高管理层仍未解决明显的违法行为，规则允许律师在有限情况下向组织外部披露信息，以防止重大损害。

这种报告机制存在的原因是，仅仅选择离开并不能履行义务。即使因提出问题而被解雇的律师，也有责任确保组织的最高管理层知晓事件及原因。这种义务是永久的。

"企业合作伙伴"的框架可能成为陷阱。越是深度嵌入业务，越难以抽身说出"我不是作为同事提供建议，而是作为你的律师告诉你，我们不能这样做"。这种姿态的转变让人不适，可能改变会议动态，但确有其必要。

归根结底，这不仅是工作问题，也不只是对组织的义务，而是涉及你的执业资格。这是唯一属于你的资源，不是任何雇主赋予或能够保护的。

"企业合作伙伴"模式虽有价值，但也存在盲区。当律师与业务顾问的界限过于模糊时，律师将承担职业风险。公司可以继续运作，而律师则要面对后果。

因此，值得定期反思：哪些是我的职责范围？我的建议在哪里结束，义务从何而来？我是否对自己的认知保持诚实？

 Lisa Lang将在2026年11月18日至20日于华盛顿特区奥姆尼岸桥酒店举行的全国大学法律顾问协会秋季继续法律教育研讨会上深入探讨这些问题。研讨会主题为"赞助研究与技术转移"。如果您是大学或学院的内部法律顾问，欢迎参加！

Lisa Lang是一位资深的内部法律顾问和行业领袖，致力于赋能同行。通过她的网站和博客《Why This, Not That™》（www.lawyerlisalang.com），她为内部律师提供见解和资源。Lisa积极参与法律社区，通过LinkedIn分享专业知识并建立有意义的联系。您可以通过lisa@lawyerlisalang.com联系她，或在LinkedIn（https://www.linkedin.com/in/lawyerlisalang/）上与她交流。
articles.summary:
In-house lawyers hear it all the time. Be a business partner. Sit at the table. Understand the business and add value beyond assessing the legal risk. 

There is no question we should. The best in-house lawyers do all of those things.

There is a tension baked into that advice, though, that nobody talks about enough. The closer you get to the business, the harder it becomes to see where the boundaries are. Not the company’s boundaries. Your ethical boundaries as a lawyer.

When do you stay quiet? When do you speak up?

The Moment That Lands Wrong

Every in-house lawyer has been in a meeting when something lands wrong. Maybe it is a business decision that brushes up against a compliance issue. Maybe it is a direction that is not clearly illegal and not clearly right, either. You weigh the room. You weigh the relationship. You weigh whether this is the moment to raise your hand or let it pass. That calculus is one of the hardest parts of the job, and no one hands you a formula for it.

The rules of professional conduct do give you a floor, though. Rule 2.1 requires every lawyer to exercise independent professional judgment and render candid advice. The comments make clear that a lawyer should not be deterred from giving that advice simply because it will be unpalatable to the client. “When do I speak up?” has an ethical answer, not just a strategic one. When your independent judgment tells you the client needs to hear it, you are obligated to say it.

Knowing What Hill To Die On

Not every issue is worth the fight. Part of being effective in-house is understanding proportionality — picking the battles that matter most and finding pragmatic solutions for the rest.

Proportionality, however, has limits. Some issues are not negotiable. Recognizing the difference between “I can live with this” and “I cannot put my name on this” is a skill that develops over time — sometimes painfully so.

Knowing When Walking Away Is Not An Option

This is where in-house practice diverges sharply from outside counsel. If an outside lawyer faces a client bent on a course of action the lawyer cannot support, withdrawal is available. For in-house lawyers, the calculus is fundamentally different. You cannot fire your only client. And even if you resign, your ethical obligations do not end when you leave the building.

Rule 1.13 recognizes this reality. The organization is your client, not the individuals directing its day-to-day operations. When an in-house lawyer knows that someone within the organization is engaged in conduct that violates a legal obligation and is likely to result in substantial injury to the organization, the lawyer is required to act. The obligation is to report up, escalating within the organization to the highest authority necessary. If the highest authority still fails to address a clear violation of law, the rules contemplate that the lawyer may, in limited circumstances, disclose information outside the organization to prevent substantial injury.

That reporting structure exists because walking away alone does not resolve the obligation. Even a lawyer who is discharged for raising these issues is required to take steps to ensure the organization’s highest authority knows what happened and why. The duty follows you.

I will not go deeper into the mechanics here. Every in-house lawyer should understand that framework and know when it applies. It is one of the most consequential aspects of our role, and one that the “business partner” model tends to obscure.

Knowing When You Have To Draw The Line

This is where the “business partner” framing can become a trap. The more embedded you are, the harder it is to step back and say, “I am not advising on this as a colleague. I am telling you as your lawyer that we cannot do this.” That shift in posture is uncomfortable. It can change the dynamic in a room. It exists for a reason.

Because at the end of the day, this is not just about your job. It is not just about your duty to the organization. It is about your license. The one thing that is entirely yours, that no employer granted you and no employer can protect for you.

The Blind Spot

The business partner model is valuable. It also has a blind spot.

When the lines between business advisor and legal counselor blur too much, the lawyer is the one who bears the professional risk. The company moves on. You carry the consequence.

So, it is worth asking yourself, regularly. What is in my lane? Where does my advice end and my obligation begin? And am I being honest with myself about the difference?

I will be exploring these questions in more depth at my session at the National Association of College and University Attorneys’s Fall 2026 CLE Workshop on Sponsored Research and Technology Transfer, November 18-20, 2026, at the Omni Shoreham Hotel in Washington, D.C. If you are an in-house lawyer for a college or university, I hope to see you there!

Lisa Lang is an accomplished in-house lawyer and thought leader dedicated to empowering fellow legal professionals. She offers insights and resources tailored for in-house counsel through her website and blog, Why This, Not That™ (www.lawyerlisalang.com). Lisa actively engages with the legal community via LinkedIn, sharing her expertise and fostering meaningful connections. You can reach her at lisa@lawyerlisalang.com, connect on LinkedIn (https://www.linkedin.com/in/lawyerlisalang/).

articles.title: Biglaw’s Latest AI Strategy: Teach Lawyers How To Be Human
articles.content:
Ed. note: Welcome to our daily feature, Quote of the Day.
You are not Atticus Finch. [Y]ou have to accept that you are in the business of sales.
— Ivan Gaviria, a corporate partner at Gunderson Dettmer, in remarks delivered during a business-development boot camp for the firm’s newest partners, as reported by Reuters. As artificial intelligence allows clients to handle more legal work themselves, law firms are training attorneys to distinguish themselves through something the bots can’t easily replicate: genuine human relationships. For lawyers hoping to build a successful book of business, simply being an excellent attorney is no longer enough, because they also need to know how to sell themselves.
